title: How to Do Things with Words
abstract: Foundational account of performative language and the distinction among locutionary, illocutionary, and perlocutionary acts. It supplies the conceptual basis for later computational treatment of requests, promises, commitments, and other communicative actions.

admission.reason: Out of scope for this reading round. It is foundational philosophical theory of performatives and illocutionary acts, but the abstract provides no empirical NLP capability, annotation evidence, extraction method, or workplace-communication evaluation that materially strengthens an authorized stream.

title: Automatically Detecting Action Items in Audio Meeting Recordings
abstract: Uses a maximum-entropy model with lexical, temporal, syntactic, semantic, and prosodic features to identify action-item-related utterances in multi-party meeting recordings annotated for action items.
venue: 7th SIGdial Workshop on Discourse and Dialogue

admission.reason: The capability is substantially covered by stronger T01 candidates that add either explicit assignment structure or source-grounded task extraction. This abstract mainly contributes utterance-level action-item detection from meeting audio features. Because identity is UNCHECKED and the otherwise similar modern action-item detection candidate 2303.16763 is VERIFIED and adds explicit local/global context modeling plus two corpora, the VERIFIED paper is preferred for the overlapping detection evidence.

title: Task-Focused Summarization of Email
abstract: Describes task-focused email summarization that identifies action items and presents extracted tasks to users, supporting conversion of email content into to-do items.

admission.reason: Topic words match, but the abstract is too summarization-oriented and provides too little evidence about how action items are defined, localized, distinguished from non-obligatory mentions, or decomposed into arguments. Its action-item contribution is also covered more specifically by the admitted email action-detection papers.

title: Segmenting Email Message Text into Zones
abstract: Introduces Zebra, an SVM system that segments email bodies into functional zones using graphic, orthographic, and lexical cues. Although not an action extractor itself, the method helps localize current-message evidence and separate it from quoted replies, signatures, and other extraneous material.

admission.reason: Topic words match only indirectly. Functional-zone segmentation can be useful preprocessing for separating quoted text, signatures, and current-message content, but the paper does not itself detect action-bearing acts, classify requests or commitments, extract action arguments, or attach deadlines. It therefore does not materially strengthen an authorized Topic 05 stream.

title: Conversation Acts in Task-Oriented Spoken Dialogue
abstract: Extends traditional speech acts into fine-grained conversation acts covering grounding, turn-taking, and task-oriented joint action, and discusses how such acts can be recognized computationally.

admission.reason: The paper is relevant conceptual background for task-oriented conversation acts, but the abstract emphasizes extending the speech-act inventory and discussing computational recognition rather than presenting sufficiently specific empirical act-classification, action-argument, or workplace-action evidence. Stronger empirical T03 evidence is available in the admitted dialogue-act modeling paper.

title: Speech Acts: An Essay in the Philosophy of Language
abstract: Develops a systematic theory of speech acts and their constitutive rules, including acts such as requesting, ordering, promising, and asserting. It is conceptual background rather than empirical extraction evidence.

admission.reason: Out of scope for this empirical reading round. It is foundational speech-act theory covering requests, orders, promises, and assertions, but the abstract provides no corpus, annotation results, computational extraction method, or workplace-communication evaluation.

title: More than Classification: A Unified Framework for Event Temporal Relation Extraction
abstract: Represents event temporal relations through relations among event start and end time points rather than treating temporal-relation extraction as an opaque class label. This structured approach is transferable to reasoning about action deadlines and temporal constraints.

admission.reason: The paper concerns general event temporal-relation extraction and a structured start/end-point representation. That is potentially useful temporal reasoning, but the abstract does not show deadline recognition, due-time or trigger semantics, or attachment of temporal expressions to requested or committed workplace actions. TimeML provides the more directly relevant event-time-linking evidence for this round.

title: Improving “Email Speech Acts” Analysis via N-gram Selection
abstract: Studies detection of email intents such as proposing a meeting and committing to a task, showing that contextual information, message preprocessing, and selected n-gram sequence features improve email-act classification.
venue: Analyzing Conversations in Text and Speech

admission.reason: The abstract is relevant to D02 but mainly contributes feature selection, preprocessing, and n-gram sequence improvements for email-act classification. The central capability is already covered by admitted direct email speech-act papers that provide stronger taxonomy, request/commitment definitions, annotation evidence, or thread-context modeling, so this would consume a reading slot for largely incremental classifier evidence.
